short.headline: India is growing old on a thin cushion
short.dek: The share of elderly has crossed 7% while income per person is still just $2,695 a year, far below the wealth that rich nations had when they aged. The engine: fertility already below replacement.
short.body: India's share of people aged 65 and over has doubled from 3.3% in 1960 to 7.1% in 2024, crossing the threshold of an ageing society. The old-age dependency ratio is set to rise from about 5 to over 12 by 2030. This is happening while GDP per capita is still only about $2,700. The median age, once 21, could hit 48 by century's end. The driver is fertility: the total fertility rate has fallen to 1.9 births per woman, below the replacement level of 2.1. Smaller generations are already born, locking in a future with fewer workers to support more elderly. The question is whether incomes can rise fast enough to build a cushion before the demographic dividend closes.

macha.heading: Okay, but what does this actually mean, macha?
macha.body: It means our country is getting older while our wallets are still thin. Think of your parents or grandparents: more of them will need care and pensions, but the working people who pay for that through taxes and family support will be fewer relative to elders. India’s income per person is just $2,695, which is like having a small savings account while the hospital bill is growing. The reason this is locked in is that families are having fewer kids—on average 1.9 per woman now. So the future has more grey hair and less money to look after it.
macha.soWhat: The crunch is coming: India must grow rich before it grows old, or prepare for a squeeze.

article.title: Is India getting old before it gets rich?
article.standfirst: India is ageing while its income per person is still low, the reverse of how today's rich countries aged. Five charts show the growing share of elderly, the rising care burden, and the fertility decline that locks it all in.
article.bodyMarkdown:
## Is India getting old before it gets rich?

Yes, and that order is the whole problem. Every society ages as it develops; the question is how much money is in the bank when it happens. Japan and Germany grew wealthy first and turned grey later, with tens of thousands of dollars of income per person to pay for pensions and hospitals. India is reaching into old age far earlier in its climb. The share of people aged 65 and above crossed 7% in 2024, while income per person stands at $2,695 a year. The elderly share is still modest, but it is rising, and the reason it will keep rising is already settled: the average Indian woman now has fewer than two children, below the level that replaces a generation. So the country will grow older on a thin cushion, and the real race is whether incomes can rise fast enough to thicken it before the working-age bulge that pays for everything begins to shrink.

## How many Indians are now 65 or older?

In 1960, only 3.3% of India’s population was 65 and above. By 2024, that share had more than doubled to 7.1%. This 7% mark is often used as a benchmark for an ageing society, and India crossed it quietly last year. A share of 7% is not alarming on its own, Japan, for instance, is at nearly 30%, but what matters is the speed of the change and the income level at which it is happening. The chart shows a gradually steepening line: the climb from 3.3% to 7.1% took 64 years, but the next 7-percentage-point rise will come much faster. The United Nations projects the older share will keep rising because the smaller generation of children born today will mean fewer young people entering the working ages. That means the share of elderly in the total pie will swell, even if nothing else changes.

## How heavy is the elder-care burden, and how fast is it growing?

The old-age dependency ratio tells us how many people aged 65 and over there are for every 100 people of working age (15–64). In 2000, India’s ratio was just 5.06. By 2030, the median United Nations projection puts it at 12.39. That is more than a doubling in three decades. A ratio of 12.39 means that for every eight working-age adults, there is roughly one elder to support, through family budgets, government pensions, or healthcare costs. This is a structural shift. The ratio is still lower than in Japan or Italy, but the pace of increase is cause for attention. One visible pattern in this data is that fertility decline drives the ratio: when fewer children are born, the pool of future workers shrinks, while the elderly population keeps growing thanks to longer lifespans. The dependency ratio is a blunt tool, it assumes every working-age person works and every older person is dependent, which is not true, but it captures the broad pressure that a society faces as it ages.

## How much income per person does India have as it ages?

India’s GDP per capita, a rough stand-in for average income, has risen from just $85 in 1960 to $2,695 in 2024. That is a thirty‑fold increase, a sign of decades of growth. But $2,695 is still a small number when set against the incomes of countries that aged before they grew rich. When Japan’s elderly share hit 7% in 1970, its GDP per capita was already around $2,000, but in today’s dollars that would be far higher. More tellingly, by the time its elderly share reached 14%, Japan had an income per head of over $40,000. India is projected to reach 14% elderly while still in the low thousands of dollars. GDP per capita is an average, not what a typical family earns. It counts everything the country produces and divides it by population. In a country with wide inequality, the median household income is much lower. Still, the chart shows that the income cushion, while growing, remains thin. The old‑before‑rich squeeze is about this mismatch: the elderly share is rising faster than the average income that could fund their support.

## How old is the typical Indian, and where is that heading?

Median age is the age that splits the population into two equal halves: half are older, half younger. In 2000, India’s median age was just 21.2 years, a very young country. By 2100, United Nations projections show it could reach 47.8 years. That is a shift from one of the world’s youngest populations to a solidly middle‑aged one. A median of 47.8 does not mean everyone is old; it means half the population would be over 48. But the share of those beyond 65 would be much larger than today. The chart’s long upward slope, from 21 to nearly 48 over a century, shows that ageing is a slow but relentless process. Even under the UN’s low‑fertility scenario, the median age rises to 57.7; under the high‑fertility scenario, it reaches 39.4. So the direction is clear regardless of possible policy changes. The critical point is that this ageing is already baked in by fertility rates today. The demographic dividend, the window when the working‑age share is large, is still open now, but it will close as the median age climbs. That is why the next two decades matter urgently for income growth.

## Why is India’s ageing now locked in?

Ageing is locked in years in advance by fertility. Once the total fertility rate falls below the replacement level of about 2.1, smaller generations are already born, and an older age structure is essentially guaranteed for decades. India’s own Sample Registration System (SRS), the government’s official survey, shows that the TFR has fallen from 2.1 births per woman in 2019 to 1.9 in 2024. That is below replacement. The difference between urban and rural is stark: urban areas have a TFR of just 1.5, while rural areas are at exactly 2.1, barely holding the line. The all‑India line dipping below 2.1 means that, on average, each generation will be smaller than the one before it. This is the engine driving the rising share of elderly. Because those smaller cohorts of children will grow up to be a smaller workforce, the ratio of elderly to working‑age people will keep climbing for at least the next few decades. The SRS data covers only 2019–2024, but it aligns with longer‑term global surveys that show India’s fertility declining for years. The takeaway is clear: the ageing train has left the station, and it is being pulled by below‑replacement fertility.

chartExplainers.title: Share of Indians aged 65 and over
chartExplainers.takeaway: The share of elderly Indians doubled from 3.3% in 1960 to 7.1% in 2024, crossing the ageing-society threshold at a low income level.
chartExplainers.detail: This line chart tracks the percentage of India’s population aged 65 and above from 1960 to 2024. The line climbs steadily, with the slope steepening in recent decades. The latest reading, 7.1% in 2024, means roughly one in fourteen Indians is now 65 or older. The world often uses 7% as the entry point into an 'ageing society', so this milestone matters—not because the share is high, but because India crossed it with an income per person of only $2,695. In the 1960s, the elderly share was just 3.3%. That slow rise is now accelerating because fertility has fallen, meaning each new generation is smaller. The chart makes visible a quiet but fundamental transformation: India is no longer a country of only young people.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The clearest sign of ageing: the older share is climbing.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Look at the line's steady rise over six decades—the slope has steepened recently.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don’t assume a 7% share means a crisis now; the alarm is about where it is heading given the income level.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: A clean single line on a phone screen with sparse year ticks works best.

chartExplainers.title: Old-age dependency ratio
chartExplainers.takeaway: India’s old-age dependency ratio is projected to more than double from 5.06 in 2000 to 12.39 by 2030, signalling a rising burden on working-age adults.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart shows the number of people aged 65 and over for every 100 people of working age (15–64). It combines historical data with United Nations projections up to 2030. The ratio starts low, at just 5.06 in 2000, but then climbs to 12.39 in 2030. That means in three decades, the potential support load on each working adult roughly doubles. In plain terms, where eight working-age people once supported less than one elder, by 2030 that group will support one full elder. The pace of change is the worrying sign—a smooth but swift rise. This is driven directly by the fertility decline: fewer children mean fewer future workers. The ratio is a simplification; many elders are still working, and not every working-age adult is employed. Yet it is the standard measure of demographic pressure, and its upward march is unambiguous.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: How many older adults each 100 working-age adults must support.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Compare the past low ratio with the sharp projected rise; a doubling in three decades is the red flag.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don’t overlook that the ratio uses a fixed boundary (65); many people stay active beyond that, but health and pension costs still concentrate.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: A single or dual-line chart with clear labels works well on mobile.

chartExplainers.title: Income per person
chartExplainers.takeaway: India’s GDP per capita has grown from $85 to $2,695 in 2024, but that is still a fraction of the wealth that rich nations had when their populations aged.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart plots India’s GDP per capita in current US dollars from 1960 to 2024. The line surges upward, reflecting decades of economic growth. The latest figure is $2,695. While the growth is impressive, the absolute level is low compared with the rich‑world ageing experience. The chart’s job is to make the 'before rich' part of the question concrete: $2,700 is the average output per person—a number that includes the output of the very wealthy—so the actual income of a typical household is even lower. Countries like Japan aged at per‑capita incomes of tens of thousands of dollars. The gap matters because pensions, healthcare, and elder care are expensive. The income line is rising, but the elderly share is rising too, and the race between the two is the central tension of the old‑before‑rich story.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The 'rich' half of the question—how wealthy India is as it ages.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Note the steep climb in dollars over 60 years, but also the absolute level: still in the low thousands.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don’t mistake this for the income of an average Indian—it is an average that includes the rich; the typical person’s income is lower.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: A line chart with large labels and a bold latest-data callout works on phones.

chartExplainers.title: Median age
chartExplainers.takeaway: India’s median age could rise from 21.2 years in 2000 to 47.8 by 2100, a slow but profound shift from youth to middle age.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart shows the median age of India’s population from 2000 to 2100, using United Nations projections. The line starts at a youthful 21.2 years in 2000 and rises steadily to 47.8 years by century’s end. A median of 47.8 means half of all Indians would be over 48, a dramatic change from today’s young country. The upward slope is uninterrupted across scenarios: even in the high-fertility variant, the median reaches 39.4, and in the low-fertility variant it hits 57.7. So ageing is not a maybe—it is a when and how fast. The median age is the simplest summary of a population’s age structure, and this chart shows that India’s structure will look very different within two generations. The demographic window of a large working-age group is now open but closing; the chart visualizes that closing.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The single number for how old the country is.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Watch the line slope upward over the century—India is moving from one of the world’s youngest populations to a middle-aged one.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don’t think median age of 47 means everyone is old; it means half are older and half younger, but the proportion of elderly will be much higher.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: A single bold line with a 100-year window stays readable if tick marks are sparse.

chartExplainers.title: The engine of ageing: fertility below replacement
chartExplainers.takeaway: India’s total fertility rate fell from 2.1 in 2019 to 1.9 in 2024, dropping below replacement and locking in future ageing.
chartExplainers.detail: This multi-line chart tracks India’s total fertility rate (TFR) from 2019 to 2024 using the government’s Sample Registration System. The all-India line drops from 2.1 to 1.9 births per woman. The dashed 2.1 line marks the replacement threshold—the level needed for a population to exactly replace itself. Below that, each generation is smaller than the last. Urban India is already far below at 1.5, while rural India sits exactly at 2.1, just holding the line. The visual makes the engine of ageing crystal clear: fewer births today mean a smaller working-age population tomorrow, and a larger share of elderly. This recent data confirms that the ageing future is already baked into the population’s age structure, regardless of what policies do next. It is the underlying cause behind the rising dependency ratios and median ages.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Ageing is locked in years in advance by fertility—and India’s is already below replacement.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Focus on the all-India line dipping below the 2.1 threshold, and contrast urban (1.5) with rural (2.1) to see where the fall is steepest.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don’t read the 2.1 rural figure as stable; it is just at replacement and has been falling too. Once it drops further, ageing accelerates.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Three lines with a clear threshold mark keep mobile reading easy—use high-contrast colors.

editorialPlanDraft.answerThesis: India is ageing while its income per person is still low, the reverse of how today's rich countries aged.
requiredConcepts: 'Getting old before getting rich' means a country's population starts ageing, a rising share of elderly, while its income per person is still low. Today's rich countries grew rich first and aged later, at high incomes; India is ageing at a much lower income per head, so it has a thinner financial cushion for pensions and elder care.

The old-age dependency ratio is the number of people aged 65 and over for every 100 people of working age (15-64); it captures how many older people each working-age adult must in effect help support through families, taxes and pensions. India's is low now but the UN data shows it edging up and set to rise far faster later.

GDP per capita is total output divided by population, used here as a rough stand-in for how rich the average Indian is, about 2,700 US dollars in 2024. It is an average, not a typical income, and it is a small fraction of the 20,000 to 40,000 dollars per head that countries like Japan or those in western Europe had reached when their populations began to age.

Median age is the age that splits the population into two equal halves; a rising median is the simplest sign of ageing. India's is still young by world standards, which is why the squeeze is a slow build rather than an immediate emergency.

Ageing is locked in years in advance by fertility: once the total fertility rate falls below the replacement level of about 2.1, smaller generations are already born, so an older age structure is essentially baked in for decades. India's SRS 2024 TFR of 1.9 (urban 1.5, rural 2.1) is the engine underneath the rising elderly share.

The demographic dividend is the window when the working-age share is high and both child and old-age dependency are low, which can lift growth; it has not closed for India yet, but below-replacement fertility means it will, and the old-before-rich question is whether incomes rise fast enough before it does.

Three sources, three jobs: SRS 2024 supplies the current, official fertility reading that drives ageing; the World Bank supplies the long arc of the elderly share and the income level; the United Nations supplies the age structure, median age and dependency ratios. They are different instruments that agree on the direction of travel.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A common demographic benchmark: when 7% or more of a population is 65 and over, a country is considered an 'ageing society'.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: India crossed this 7% line in 2024, but it did so at a far lower income level than countries like Japan did decades ago.

proseRules: No outside facts — every number must come from lockedNumbers.
No calculations unless the evidence packet supplies the derived number.

evidence.question: Is India getting old before it gets rich?

theme.label: People and demography
readerQuestions: Is the trend rising, falling, or slowing?
What is the age or sex structure behind the total?
What does this change for jobs, schools, care, and families?

selectionRules: Start from the page question, not from the indicator name.
Choose the smallest set of visuals that explains scale, trend, structure, comparison, and caveat.
Prefer mobile-friendly charts: line charts with sparse ticks, horizontal bars, share strips, pyramids only when essential, and no dense tables.
Use one strong pull quote only when the evidence supports it with a number.
Add glossary blocks for technical terms that normal readers may not know.
caveats: Use only figures present in lockedNumbers or sourceSummaries.
If a related theme indicator is present, you may use it for context, but do not pretend it is the main answer.
If source coverage is thin, say so directly.
Do not compare states, districts, or cities unless the evidence packet contains those geographies.
forbiddenClaims: Do not infer causality from a trend unless the evidence explicitly supports it.
Do not cite a source that is not present in sourceSummaries.
